newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: U.S. official due in Seoul as tensions mount.
newsitem.headline: U.S. official due in Seoul as tensions mount.

text.p: The United States said on Tuesday it was sending a senior official to South Korea as tensions rise over the intrusion of a North Korean submarine and Pyongyang's arrest of a U.S. citizen on spy charges.
South Korea's Yonhap news agency quoted a Seoul foreign ministry official as saying Winston Lord was likely to "strongly denounce" Pyongyang during a three-day visit starting on Thursday.
There have been mounting attacks on the United States in the local media and parliament over its perceived weak response to the submarine intrusion last month.
Yonhap quoted the official as saying Lord would seek to reassure South Korea the United States was not going soft on North Korea.

"The visit by Lord to Seoul seems to focus on dispelling doubts about America's willingness to tackle North Korea," the unnamed official was quoted as saying. "In that sense, it is very likely that Lord will strongly denounce North Korea."
The foreign ministry spokesman was not immediately available for comment.
Pyongyang maintains the submarine drifted south after developing engine problems.

South Korea says it was landing commandos in preparation for wider military action. Of 26 North Koreans who came ashore, 22 have been killed or found dead, and Pyongyang has vowed "merciless retaliation".
On Sunday Pyongyang said it had arrested a U.S. citizen on charges of spying for South Korea. Washington has demanded North Korea free the man.
The U.S. embassy in Seoul said in a statement that Lord, Assistant Secretary of State for East Asia and Pacific Affairs, would discuss "ramifications of the recent submarine incident".

Some South Koreans feel betrayed by Washington's restrained response to the incursion and believe that by urging both North and South Korea to cool passions, the United States is trying to appear even-handed instead of backing its ally.
The United States maintains 37,000 troops in South Korea, but Seoul constantly frets that Washington is trying to cut secret deals with Pyongyang behind its back.

Local newspapers have lashed out at U.S. President Bill Clinton, accusing him of a policy of appeasement towards North Korea to try to keep the peace on the Korean peninsula at any cost before presidential elections.
"The Korea-U.S. relationship has now run aground on the rocks of emotionalism, haughtiness, distrust and lack of dialogue," the Chosun Ilbo daily said last week.
It accused Washington of "keeping a distance from South Korea" and "moving towards a middle-of-the-road position".
The U.N. Command on Tuesday rebuked North Korea over the incursion and warned Pyongyang against retaliating.

An officer of the U.S.-led command, which monitors a ceasefire that ended the 1950-53 Korean War, delivered the protest in a letter at the border village of Panmunjom, according to a U.N. Command statement.
"The letter advised the North that the body of evidence showed the infiltration to be deliberate," the letter said.

The letter warned the Korean People's Army against further violations of the ceasefire accord and "reminded the KPA that 'retaliating' against (South Korea) also violates the agreement", the statement added.
Later, at a second border meeting called by North Korea, the protest letter was returned.
